Additive Log-Ratio Transform

Source: R/log_ratio_transforms.r
alr.Rd

The log of every feature's abundance relative to one chosen feature, the denominator: Aitchison's additive log ratio (alr).

Usage

alr(counts, denominator, margin = 1L, pseudocount = NULL, cpus = n_cpus())

Arguments

counts

A numeric matrix of non-negative abundances (samples \(\times\) features), or any of the objects listed under Input Types. Counts, proportions, and the output of a zero replacement are all accepted: each sample's scale cancels out of the log ratios.

denominator

The feature to divide by: its name, or its (1-based) index among the features, or a logical vector with one TRUE. Required. Choose a feature that is present in every sample and abundant and stable across them, since every coordinate is relative to it.

margin

The margin containing samples. 1 if samples are rows, 2 if samples are columns. Ignored when counts is a special object class (e.g. phyloseq). Default: 1

pseudocount

Added to every value before taking logs. NULL (the default) adds nothing when counts has no zeros, and otherwise uses half the smallest non-zero value, with a warning. See Pseudocount.

cpus

How many parallel processing threads should be used. The default, n_cpus(), will use all logical CPU cores.

Value

A dense numeric matrix of the \(D - 1\) coordinates, in the orientation of counts: samples \(\times\) coordinates for margin = 1, coordinates \(\times\) samples for margin = 2 (and for a single sample given as a vector). Sample names are kept. Each coordinate is named after its numerator feature, in the order of counts; features without names give alr1, alr2, ..., numbered by their position in counts (so denominator = 2 of 4 gives alr1, alr3, alr4). Attributes:

  • method: 'alr'.

  • denominator: the denominator feature's name, or its index when the features have no names.

  • pseudocount: the pseudocount used (0 for none).

Details

For a sample \(x\) of \(D\) features and denominator \(x_d\), $$\mathrm{alr}(x) = \left[\log\frac{x_j + c}{x_d + c}\right]_{j \neq d}$$ with \(c\) the pseudocount (natural logs). The coordinates are easy to interpret (everything relative to one feature) and are what multinomial regression models use, but the transform is not an isometry: Euclidean distances between alr coordinates are not Aitchison distances. For distances, use aitchison(); for orthonormal coordinates, ilr(). The centered log ratio is normalize(counts, 'clr') (or norm = 'clr' in any function that takes norm).

alr(x + c, d) here equals scikit-bio's alr(x + c, ref_idx = d - 1) exactly. scikit-bio defaults to the first feature and compositions::alr() to the last: ecodive has no default, because the choice shapes every coordinate.

The result feeds straight into pca(), rda(), lda(), envfit() and euclidean(), which take negative values with norm = 'none'.

Same names in other packages: compositions::alr() (the last part as denominator) and robCompositions::addLR() compute the same transform. Whichever package was attached last masks the other's alr(); write ecodive::alr() to be sure.

Input Types

The counts parameter is designed to accept a simple numeric matrix, but seamlessly supports objects from the following biological data packages:

  • phyloseq

  • rbiom

  • SummarizedExperiment

  • TreeSummarizedExperiment

For large datasets, standard matrix operations may be slow. See vignette('performance') for details on using optimized formats (e.g. sparse matrices) and parallel processing.

Pseudocount

Logs of zero are undefined, so zeros need replacing first. The pseudocount is added to every value (not only to zeros), as in normalize(norm = 'clr'). With pseudocount = NULL (the default), no pseudocount is used when counts has no zeros; otherwise half the smallest non-zero value is, with a warning. To avoid a pseudocount, replace the zeros first with replace_zeros(): its result has none.

The choice of pseudocount is not neutral: it can distort the results, especially for sparse tables. See aitchison() for references.

References

Aitchison, J. (1986). The Statistical Analysis of Compositional Data. Chapman & Hall.

See also

ilr(), normalize() ('clr' and 'rclr'), aitchison()

Examples

    # Relative to the first feature
    x <- alr(ex_counts, denominator = 1, pseudocount = 1)
    x[1:3, 1:3]
#>        Bacteroides Corynebacterium Haemophilus
#> Saliva   -3.995138       -5.093750   0.1047468
#> Gums     -5.067646       -6.677083  -2.1997466
#> Nose     -2.036882        3.077112  -2.0368819
    attr(x, 'denominator')
#> [1] "Streptococcus"

    # The same as the log ratios themselves
    all.equal(
      unname(x[, 1]),
      unname(log((ex_counts[, 2] + 1) / (ex_counts[, 1] + 1))) )
#> [1] TRUE
